extraction.name: MATH (Mathematics Aptitude Test of Heuristics)
extraction.description: A dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems, split into 7,500 training and 5,000 test problems. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution and a final boxed answer. Problems cover seven subjects and are tagged with difficulty levels from 1 to 5. Mathematical notation is represented in LaTeX, and graphical figures are represented in Asymptote code.
extraction.creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Bums, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt
extraction.citeAs: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Bums, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, and Jacob Steinhardt. Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. NeurIPS 2021 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks. arXiv:2103.03874v2.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors collected problems from mathematics competitions, including AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME. Many problems can be collected from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. The paper describes MATH as carefully curated by the competition mathematics community.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Problems from mathematics competitions, including AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME, available through the Art of Problem Solving competition archive at aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. The paper states that MATH problems are created by the Mathematical Association of America.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset is divided into 7,500 training problems and 5,000 test problems.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions are consistently formatted using LaTeX and Asymptote. Figures are encoded as Asymptote code rather than raster images. Final boxed answers follow consistent formatting rules: probabilities are simplified fractions; matrix entry fractions use x/y while other fractions use the LaTeX fraction command; coefficients omit multiplication symbols; variables are alphabetically ordered; and polynomials are expressed in decreasing degree order.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each problem includes a step-by-step solution and a final answer delimited by the LaTeX boxed command. Problems are categorized into Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus. Difficulty levels follow AoPS and range from 1, the easiest problems within a subject for humans, to 5, the hardest. The paper does not specify how individual solutions were authored.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Answer normalization supports exact-match evaluation by treating equivalent fraction and parenthesis encodings as equivalent, ignoring spaces, permitting units to be included or omitted, recognizing common equivalent numerical representations, and permitting different factor orderings for factorized polynomials. The paper states that these rules cover nearly all practical ways in which generated and reference answers can be equivalent.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper notes that even 40% model accuracy would have ramifications for cheating on homework. The authors do not intend the dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. They state that solving MATH with machine learning would have profound practical and intellectual significance because of the broad applicability of mathematics.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The answer-formatting rules cover nearly all, rather than all, practical forms of answer equivalence. The authors explicitly state that training models to help students cheat on mathematics exams is not an intended use.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability and forecasting reasoning capabilities. The training split supports learning problem-solving heuristics and fine-tuning models to generate final answers and step-by-step solutions; the test split supports exact-match evaluation and analysis across subjects and difficulty levels. The authors do not intend use for training models that facilitate cheating on mathematics exams.
